label: text
content: ## Burrows Wheeler Transform (BWT)

label: text
content: The BWT applies a reversible transformation to a block of input text. The transformation does not itself compress the data, but reorders it to make it easy to compress with simple algorithms such as move-to-front coding

label: text
content: Original publication: Burrows & Wheeler, 1994

label: text
content: ## The significance of the BWT for most of the world is its use for data compression

label: text
content: Leads to a block-sorted data structure (runs of repeated characters)

label: text
content: E. g., basis for the bzip2 compression algorithm

label: text
content: ## Basis for many of the read mapping algorithms in common use today

label: text
content: The obtained block-sorted data structure is also well suited to searching short strings in a larger text (here: reads in a genome)

label: text
content: The FM index uses the BWT, the suffix array and additional data structures to enable search with time linear in the length of the search string (length of the read! see Ferragina & Manzini, 20000000000

label: text
content: - Construct a tally table: ("tally" $\approx$ counter)

label: text
content: Precalculate the number of each specific character in L up to every row

label: text
content: (In general, we can substract one from the tally to obtain the zero-based B-rank; i.e., $B$-rank = tally - 1)$

content: ## FM Index - Tally Table

label: text
content: - Say we are search for P=abra

label: text
content: - After we have found all rows beginning with a in the first step,we need to find rows with r in the L column

label: text
content: - Say the range of rows is $[i,j]$

label: text
content: - We look in the tally table in row i - 1. No occurences of r before i!

label: text
content: - Now look in the tally table row $j$. Two occurrences of $r$ at $j!$

label: text
content:
- Therefore, we know that (only) $r_{0}$ and $r_1$ occur in $\mathbf{L}$ in the range $[i,j]$

$Two lookups instead of$ O(|T|)$ !

content: - For instance, to calculate the rank of the A near the $\leftarrow$ ???

label: text
content: - We can go to the previous checkpoint and count the number of A's that we encounter from there to the position we are interested in: $ 11111111113+1=1114

label: text
content: - Or: We can go to the next checkpoint and subtract the number of A's that we encounter along the way: $ 1115-1=11111114

content: ## FM Index - Tally Table

content: - Assuming we space the check point rows a constant number of rows away from one another (k is constant): $\mathcal{O}(1)$ for instance, 50 rows then lookups are still $\mathcal{O}(1)$ rather than $|T|$
